title: The Ship That Was Never Quite the Same
paragraphs: Plutarch records that the Athenians preserved the ship on which Theseus had returned from Crete, removing planks as they decayed and fitting sound timber in their place. Philosophers who later examined the story disagreed about whether, after the last original plank had gone, the vessel was still the same ship.

Those who answered yes pointed to continuity: at no moment did anyone abandon the ship, and each repair was too small to destroy its identity. A river, after all remains a river although none of its water stays. Those who answered no argued that identity depends on the original matter, so a ship built entirely of new wood is, strictly speaking, a replica.

Thomas Hobbes sharpened the puzzle in the seventeenth century by adding a rival claimant. Suppose, he said, that someone collected the discarded planks and reassembled them in their original order. Two ships would then exist, and each would have a plausible claim to be the original. Continuity of form favours the repaired vessel, whereas continuity of material favours the reassembled one.

The difficulty is not that the evidence is missing, but that the word same is doing two jobs. In one sense it asks whether a thing has persisted through time; in another it asks whether it is made of the same stuff. Ordinary language usually keeps these questions apart because, in everyday life, they rarely collide. The ship forces them into conflict.

Perhaps that is why the puzzle has survived for nearly two thousand years. It does not hide a secret fact waiting to be found; it reveals that our concept of identity was never as tidy as it seemed. Every person who has changed over the years while still insisting on being the same self has a stake in the answer. Whichever answer we choose, we should admit exactly what it costs us.
